description: One cup of rolled oats weighs 89 grams, spooned and levelled. Convert rolled oats between cups, grams, and tablespoons, with the table and worked examples.

steps: Multiply by the weight of one cup: 2 × 89 g.
examples.title: 2 cups of rolled oats to grams

steps: Divide by the weight of one cup: 100 ÷ 89.
examples.title: 100 g of rolled oats to cups

faqs.answer: 89 grams, when the cup is spooned and levelled. That is the figure on King Arthur Baking's ingredient weight chart for old-fashioned or quick-cooking oats.
faqs.question: How many grams are in a cup of rolled oats?

faqs.answer: Because King Arthur's own brand of rolled oats weighs 113 grams per cup. It is a thicker-cut product. The 89-gram figure is for standard old-fashioned or quick-cooking oats, which is what most people buy. If your oats are thick-cut, they will weigh more per cup.
faqs.question: Why do some charts say 113 g per cup?

faqs.answer: No. Steel-cut oats are denser and weigh more per cup. King Arthur lists them at 70 grams per half cup, so a cup is 140 grams. Much heavier than a cup of rolled oats at 89 grams.
faqs.question: Do steel-cut oats weigh the same as rolled oats?

faqs.answer: About 2.25 cups. 200 ÷ 89 = 2.25 cups, which is 2 cups plus 1/4 cup.
faqs.question: How many cups is 200 g of rolled oats?

faqs.answer: Yes. King Arthur lists old-fashioned and quick-cooking oats at the same weight: 89 grams per cup. Quick oats are just rolled thinner and cut smaller, so they cook faster.
faqs.question: Do quick-cooking oats weigh the same as old-fashioned oats?

felicityNote: Overnight oats taught me to weigh them. One scooped cup too many and the jar comes out dry. The scale keeps the ratio right.

parts.meaning: The volume in the recipe, measured spooned and levelled.
The grams in one cup of old-fashioned or quick-cooking oats, from King Arthur Baking's chart.

howToSteps.name: Stir the oats
howToSteps.text: Give the oats a stir in the bag or jar first. Oats settle in storage, and the flakes at the bottom pack tighter than the ones on top.

howToSteps.name: Spoon them into the cup
howToSteps.text: Spoon the oats into the measuring cup until it heaps over the top. Do not scoop with the cup itself. Scooping packs the flakes down.

howToSteps.name: Level it off
howToSteps.text: Sweep the flat edge of a knife across the rim of the cup, back into the bag. The cup is now level and holds one cup, 89 grams.

howToSteps.name: Convert or weigh
howToSteps.text: Weigh the oats if you have a scale: one level cup should read 89 grams. Or use the converter above. Cups times 89 is grams, grams divided by 89 is cups.

name: Rolled Oats
sourceNote: King Arthur Baking lists old-fashioned or quick-cooking oats at 89 g per cup (3 1/8 oz).
title: Rolled Oats Cups to Grams Converter
tutorial: A cup of rolled oats weighs 89 grams. That is light for a cup. Oats are flat flakes with a lot of air between them, so the cup holds less than you would expect. A cup of flour weighs 120 grams. A cup of oats weighs 89.

The number comes from King Arthur Baking's chart: 89 grams per cup for old-fashioned or quick-cooking oats, spooned and levelled. Spoon the oats into the cup and level it off. Oats settle in the bag, so a scooped cup packs in more than a spooned one.

There is one number that trips people up. King Arthur's own brand of rolled oats weighs 113 grams per cup. It is a thicker cut than the standard oats most shops sell. The 89-gram figure is for standard old-fashioned or quick-cooking oats, which is what most people buy. If your oats look thick and hearty, they may weigh more than 89 grams a cup. The scale settles it.

Use the converter in either direction. Cups become grams for the scale, grams become cups when you are working without one. The anchors are easy: half a cup is about 45 grams, two cups is 178 grams. Overnight oats and flapjacks mostly live on those numbers.

One thing worth knowing: steel-cut oats weigh more per cup than rolled oats. King Arthur lists steel-cut oats at 70 grams per half cup, so a full cup is 140 grams. They are dense little pieces of whole oat, not flakes, so they pack tighter. Do not swap them cup for cup. Use the weight.
